title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models
authors: Aravindan Kamatchi Sundaram, B. Pabitramohan Prusty, Rohit Batra
abstract: Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.

infographic.key_insight: This review traces how materials information extraction has evolved from rule-based pipelines to multimodal LLMs and agentic systems supporting materials discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated literature extraction can populate materials databases and knowledge graphs and support research assistants and autonomous laboratory workflows.
method: Reviews rule-based, NLP, transformer-encoder, LLM and agentic extraction approaches.
Examines extraction from text, tables and figures.
Assesses generated datasets, extraction accuracy, computational costs and pipeline design.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a critical assessment of datasets, accuracy and costs, but reports no quantitative results and highlights scarce reliable benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Reliable sample-level linking of structure, properties, processing and performance remains an open challenge.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models

title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
authors: Yazhuo Liu, Kunqing Ding, Xiaoguo Gong, Zifeng Wang, Yichen Yang, Yifeng Che
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.

infographic.key_insight: GBClaw links agentic AI-driven atomistic simulations with mechanistic analysis, revealing how defect hierarchies and metastable grain boundary structures influence sliding resistance in nickel.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding how complex grain boundaries resist sliding could help guide microstructure design for polycrystalline materials.
method: Coordinate LLM-based specialist agents through an orchestrator, domain tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory.
Dynamically replan simulations and refine workflows to characterize boundary defects and deformation modes.
Compare sliding with and without secondary misfit dislocations, then investigate anomalies through researcher-guided calculations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 14 general asymmetric tilt grain boundaries in nickel, simulations revealed diverse deformation modes and substantial shear-strength differences associated with secondary misfit dislocations.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to 14 nickel boundaries, and the anomalous high-resistance mechanism required researcher-guided follow-up rather than fully autonomous discovery.
infographic.paper_title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery

title: Multiscale Modeling of Zr Corrosion: Predicting Microstructures of Oxide Films
authors: K. Starkey, L. Kahle, M. Christensen, V. Eyert, A. El-Azab, C. B. Geller
abstract: A first-principles-informed multiscale modeling approach is reported for oxide formation during corrosion of zirconium. The present simulations reproduce the columnar corrosion film microstructure and grain size distribution seen in micrographs of oxidized Zr surfaces. This structural feature emerges from a hexagonal ZrO layer adjacent to the $α$-Zr/ZrO$_{2-x}$ interface, which is dynamically stabilized by continuous heterogeneous grain nucleation and grain boundary mass diffusion. This ZrO layer is identified as a significant oxygen diffusion barrier and a potential contributor to sub-parabolic pretransition corrosion kinetics. The simulations also reproduce the undulatory nature of the metal/oxide interface, leading to regions with tensile stress components capable of nucleating cracks, despite the overall state of compressive hydrostatic stress within the oxide film. First principles density functional theory (DFT) computations of fundamental ZrO$_x$ properties were combined with molecular dynamics simulations using a machine-learned potential based on a DFT training set to provide extensive input to an advanced phase field model for oxide formation and its microstructure, as implemented in the new MedeA PhaseField module. The phase field simulations reported herein incorporated computed stoichiometry-dependent thermochemical data, anisotropic elastic properties, interface energies, bulk and grain boundary mass transport processes, multiphase heterogeneous grain nucleation, and strain energy-dependent phase stabilities.

infographic.key_insight: Multiscale simulations identify a dynamically stabilized hexagonal ZrO interlayer that shapes columnar oxide growth and acts as a significant oxygen diffusion barrier during zirconium corrosion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model links oxide microstructure, oxygen transport, and local tensile stresses to corrosion kinetics and potential crack initiation in zirconium components.
method: Compute ZrOₓ thermochemical and elastic properties using first-principles DFT.
Use molecular dynamics with a DFT-trained machine-learned potential to supply additional model inputs.
Simulate oxide growth in MedeA PhaseField with heterogeneous nucleation, mass transport, interface energies, and strain-dependent phase stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports reproduction of columnar oxide microstructures and grain-size distributions observed in micrographs, along with an undulating metal/oxide interface.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative validation errors, and the ZrO layer’s contribution to sub-parabolic corrosion kinetics remains a proposed mechanism.
infographic.paper_title: Multiscale Modeling of Zr Corrosion: Predicting Microstructures of Oxide Films

title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins
authors: Pablo Luna Falcon, Jason Mayeur, Amirkoushyar Ziabari, Vincent Paquit, Patxi Fernandez-Zelaia
abstract: Metal additive manufacturing (AM) offers substantial advantages to the fabrication of complex structural components, but its widespread adoption is slowed due to complexities in the process-structure-property relations which is the cause for uncertainty and drives risk. Accurately quantifying these complex relations solely via experimental workflows is time consuming and costly. Integrated computational materials and engineering (ICME) frameworks address this challenge by leveraging advanced computational tools, such as crystal plasticity finite element models (CPFEM), to predict critical mechanical properties directly from microstructural data. However, these frameworks require a large datasets that are often difficult to obtain, and their predictive accuracy depends on the availability of realistic AM microstructure representations. Generative deep learning models are a promising approach towards synthesizing AM microstructures which contain complex morphological and crystallographic features. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), in particular, show a strong potential to capture the inherent complexities of AM structures. In this work, we demonstrate that DDPMs can reliably synthesize digital-twin orientation-imaging micrographs, and we support this claim with quantitative evidence of the fidelity of the generated samples. Additionally, we establish a classifier-free guidance framework for solving complex inverse problems such as property-to-structure and process-to-structure mappings, and we showcase a potential application on a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification problem. Our work highlights the potential of AI-based generative modeling as a key component of computational frameworks for accelerating AM materials qualification and certification.

infographic.key_insight: Denoising diffusion models generate realistic additive-manufacturing orientation micrographs and support inverse mappings from properties or processing conditions to microstructure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Synthetic microstructures could strengthen digital-twin workflows and help accelerate additive-manufacturing materials qualification.
method: Use denoising diffusion probabilistic models to synthesize orientation-imaging micrographs.
Apply classifier-free guidance to property-to-structure and process-to-structure inverse problems.
Demonstrate a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification application.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports quantitative evidence of generated-sample fidelity but does not specify dataset sizes, evaluation metrics, or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Micrograph fidelity alone does not establish accurate downstream mechanical predictions; validation across processing conditions remains important.
infographic.paper_title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins

title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
authors: Ouns El Harzli, Jelle Bor, Linde Wester, Leonid Zhukov, Hanl Park, Jean-François Bobier
abstract: We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode materials under SOFC and SOEC deployment scenarios informed by public technical targets and electrolyser deployment data.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum impurity solvers could help screen strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials by resolving interface energetics and electronic transport beyond practical classical limits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework links microscopic material properties to solid oxide fuel cell and electrolyser performance through electrode transport, surface exchange, microstructure, and thickness.
method: Use DFT to shortlist materials and construct atomistic electrode–electrolyte interface models.
Apply GW+DMFT or SEET embedding with quantum impurity solvers for finite-temperature Green’s functions.
Connect vacancy energetics and conductivity to continuum electrode models and deployment-based value estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract outlines convergence benchmarks against classical solvers and illustrative logical-qubit counts, rather than reporting demonstrated quantum advantage.
infographic.watch_item: Practical feasibility depends on thermal-state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs that require a complete resource assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation

title: STAR-XPC: Set Transformer for Estimating X-ray Transmission in Polymer Composites
authors: Can Erer, H. Birkan Yilmaz, Nebahat Aral
abstract: Evaluating the energy transmission ratio of an X-ray beam through a polymer composite is a challenging task in radiation shielding studies. The reference solution with Monte Carlo transport simulation is highly accurate but computationally expensive: each of our reference simulations is capped at $4\times10^9$ photon histories and a 20,000 s (over 5 hours) time limit, while closed-form analytical methods fail to represent such complex scenarios. We present an artificial neural network model that maps the unordered multi-set of molecular constituents, their mass fractions, and four bulk physical descriptors directly to the transmission ratio $I(t)/I_0$ in 1-3 milliseconds. The model is a Set Transformer, which makes it permutation invariant by construction and accepts mixtures of different sizes up to 11 constituents within a fixed-size padded set. Each constituent is embedded with a chemistry-pretrained transformer language model, ChemBERTa. In our proposed method, training data are produced by an automated PENELOPE/penEasy pipeline using the radiation source at 30, 80, 100, and 120 kV tube voltages over polyethylene-based shielding composite slabs of thicknesses spanning 0.15-2.5 mm. After preprocessing, the dataset contains $n = 4697$ simulated configurations on which a leakage-free, jointly stratified 10-fold cross-validation is performed, attaining mean squared error MSE = $(1.12 \pm 0.56)\times10^{-4}$, normalized-MSE percentage NMSE% = 0.0294% $\pm$ 0.0147%, and $R^2 = 0.9988$. The corresponding per-sample percentage errors give an alpha-trimmed ($α= 0.10$) absolute percentage error (APE) of 1.66% and a median APE of 1.15%. Our model's inference is several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying Monte Carlo simulation (sub-millisecond per query vs. several hours for the reference run) with effective accuracy in predicting $I(t)/I_0$.

infographic.key_insight: STAR-XPC uses a Set Transformer to predict X-ray transmission through polymer composites in milliseconds with high agreement to Monte Carlo simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model could accelerate radiation-shielding material screening by reducing reliance on computationally expensive transport simulations.
method: Represent up to 11 molecular constituents using ChemBERTa embeddings and mass fractions.
Combine unordered constituent sets with four bulk physical descriptors in a permutation-invariant Set Transformer.

infographic.evidence_signal: On 4,697 simulated configurations, leakage-free, jointly stratified 10-fold cross-validation achieved R² = 0.9988, MSE = (1.12 ± 0.56) × 10⁻⁴, and median absolute percentage error of 1.15%.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is simulation-based; performance beyond the studied polyethylene-based composites, four tube voltages spanning 30–120 kV, and 0.15–2.5 mm thicknesses remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: STAR-XPC: Set Transformer for Estimating X-ray Transmission in Polymer Composites

title: First-principles modeling of ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys
authors: Daniil M. Khodachenko, Andrei V. Ruban, Franco Moitzi, Oleg E. Peil, Vsevolod I. Razumovskiy
abstract: The atomic ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys strongly influences their magnetic properties and mechanical behavior. While general features of long-range atomic ordering are known from the experimentally established phase diagram in this composition range, detailed atomic configurations and driving forces behind them remain speculative. Here, we address this gap by using effective cluster interactions (ECI) obtained from density functional theory (DFT) calculations and subsequent statistical thermodynamics modeling to unravel the interplay between magnetism, composition, and temperature in body-centered cubic (bcc) Fe-Si alloys up to 20 at% Si. Our analysis reveals that the ordering behavior is governed by a strong coupling between magnetic order, lattice expansion, and Si concentration, with specific ECI shells switching sign or magnitude as the magnetic state changes, which is reflected in the phase equilibria and ordering behavior of Fe-Si alloys. In particular, we demonstrate that D0$_3$ ordering is, in fact, primary in the totally ordered ferromagnetic state, while the B2 type of ordering is promoted in the paramagnetic state at elevated temperatures. The temperature-dependent evolution of these ordering patterns, obtained from Monte Carlo simulations based on the magnetically resolved ECIs, reproduces the experimentally observed phase equilibria and short-range order characteristics. By explicitly linking the magnetic state with the effective interactions and macroscopic phase behavior, this work establishes a predictive framework for an ab initio-based description of ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys and highlights the decisive role of magnetism in ordering phenomena in this system.

infographic.key_insight: Magnetism governs ordering in Fe-rich Fe–Si alloys: D0₃ ordering dominates in the fully ordered ferromagnetic state, while paramagnetism promotes B2 ordering at elevated temperatures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Linking magnetism, composition, and temperature to atomic ordering could guide processing of Fe–Si alloys whose magnetic and mechanical properties depend on atomic arrangement.
method: Calculate magnetically resolved effective cluster interactions using density functional theory.
Analyze how magnetic state, lattice expansion, and Si concentration alter ordering interactions.
Use Monte Carlo simulations to predict temperature-dependent ordering and phase equilibria.
infographic.evidence_signal: For bcc Fe–Si alloys up to 20 at% Si, the simulations reproduce experimentally observed phase equilibria and short-range-order characteristics.
infographic.watch_item: The reported scope is bcc alloys up to 20 at% Si; predictions beyond this range require validation.
infographic.paper_title: First-principles modeling of ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys

title: Instability-driven segregation of V group transition metals on HEB$_2$ grain boundaries influencing enhanced mechanical properties
authors: Daniil Alekseev, Viktor S. Baidyshev, Alexander G. Kvashnin
abstract: Five metals share a common sublattice in the (Hf,Ta,Ti,Nb,Zr)B$_2$ (HEB$_2$). Most high-entropy materials are produced as polycrystalline materials in the form of sintered ceramics. The question of which metal species are located at grain boundaries is still unknown. Here, we calculated the grain-boundary energy $γ_{GB}$ of four types of boundaries in five binary diborides and HEB$_2$ using density functional theory (DFT). We analyzed the bonding at these boundaries using COHP and sampled cation segregation at six boundaries of HEB$_2$, ordered and general, using Monte Carlo / molecular dynamics with a MACE potential that was fine-tuned for this system. According to our results $γ_{GB}$ splits by group: the group V diborides NbB$_2$ and TaB$_2$ form boundaries with about half the energy of the group IV at three of the four types of GBs, ranging from 0.8 to 2.7 compared to 2.5--4.8~J/m$^2$. COHP shows a significant difference at the Fermi level, namely the Me--B bonds of NbB$_2$ and TaB$_2$ are antibonding at Fermi energy ($E_F$) in the bulk but bonding at the GB, while their integrated strength hardly changes. In HEB$_2$ the segregation follows a similar pattern: Nb and Ta are enriched at five of the six grain boundaries, including general boundaries, up to 23--35~at.\% at 2000~K, although the size of the atoms would favor Zr and Hf in the expanded sites. A segregated $Σ193$ grain boundary can withstand 26 against 20~GPa for a random boundary in tension at 300~K. The grain boundaries of HEB$_2$ are composed of group V metals, as suggested by the boundary energies of binaries compounds and their bonding at the Fermi level. Grain boundaries of the (Hf,Ta,Ti,Nb,Zr)B$_2$ preferentially include Nb and Ta. This lowers the grain boundary energy and strengthens the boundaries. This consists of the lower boundary energy and changes Fermi level bonding in NbB$_2$ and TaB$_2$.

infographic.key_insight: Nb and Ta preferentially segregate to grain boundaries in (Hf,Ta,Ti,Nb,Zr)B₂, linking group V bonding behavior to lower boundary energies and greater boundary strength.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling grain-boundary chemistry could help strengthen high-entropy diboride ceramics without changing their overall composition.
method: DFT calculations of four grain-boundary types in five binary diborides and HEB₂.
COHP analysis of metal–boron bonding at grain boundaries.
Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics sampling of six HEB₂ boundaries using a fine-tuned MACE potential.
infographic.evidence_signal: Nb and Ta enrichment occurred at five of six sampled boundaries at 2000 K; at 300 K, a segregated Σ193 boundary sustained 26 GPa in tension versus 20 GPa for a chemically random boundary.
infographic.watch_item: The computational results cover selected boundaries and require experimental validation before extrapolation to bulk ceramic performance.
infographic.paper_title: Instability-driven segregation of V group transition metals on HEB$_2$ grain boundaries influencing enhanced mechanical properties

title: Nitrogen vacancy cluster-mediated ferroelectric domain growth in wurtzite AlN
authors: Zijian Zhou, Kan-Hao Xue, Ziqi Pang, Heng Yu, Shanzhong Xie, Hang Liu
abstract: Aluminum nitride-based ferroelectrics combine high remanent polarization, thermal stability, weak size effects, a wide bandgap and back-end process compatibility, making them promising for high density non-volatile memory. However, their high coercive field ($E_\mathrm{c}$) and unclear polarization switching mechanism limit further applications. Theoretical predictions indicate preferential reversed domain growth along the polar axis, whereas experiments show nearly isotropic growth or preferential growth perpendicular to this axis. Here, we combine density functional theory, Deep Potential molecular dynamics and experimental characterization to determine how nitrogen vacancies ($V_\mathrm{N}$) regulate domain growth and $E_\mathrm{c}$. In ideal crystal, strong lattice coupling along the polar axis drives preferential domain growth in this direction. $V_\mathrm{N}$ locally weakens this coupling and promotes polarization nucleation. The spatial distribution of $V_\mathrm{N}$ and the temporal sequence of vacancy induced switching jointly determine the direction and morphology of reversed domain growth. We further show that scandium doping promotes $V_\mathrm{N}$ formation, thereby enhancing defect mediated nucleation and reducing $E_\mathrm{c}$. These findings establish a multiscale mechanism governing thin-film domain-growth kinetics and macroscopic $E_\mathrm{c}$, reconciling experimental observations with ideal crystal simulations and providing defect engineering principles for low-voltage, reliable and scalable ferroelectric devices.

infographic.key_insight: Nitrogen vacancies locally weaken polar-axis lattice coupling in wurtzite AlN, enabling nucleation and redirecting ferroelectric domain growth according to vacancy distribution and switching sequence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineering nitrogen vacancies, whose formation is promoted by scandium doping, could lower coercive fields and support low-voltage AlN-based ferroelectric memory.
method: Density functional theory for atomic-scale mechanisms
Deep Potential molecular dynamics for domain-growth kinetics
Experimental characterization to connect simulations with observed behavior
infographic.evidence_signal: The combined calculations, simulations and experiments link vacancy-mediated switching to domain-growth patterns that differ from ideal-crystal predictions, although the abstract reports no numerical performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Device implementation requires control of vacancy distribution; the abstract does not establish an optimal defect concentration or quantify reliability trade-offs.
infographic.paper_title: Nitrogen vacancy cluster-mediated ferroelectric domain growth in wurtzite AlN

title: Universal Synthesis of Large-Area Hybrid Perovskite Monolayers Enabling Lithography-Free, Low-Static-Power Optoelectronics
authors: Shankeerthan Kalyanasundaram, Swarit Dwivedi, Sanje Mahasivam, Christopher R. McNeill, Sudha Mokkapati
abstract: Solution-phase synthesis of monolayer hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites is constrained by rapid out-of-plane crystal growth, uncontrolled nucleation, and strong interlayer aggregation, yielding flakes of only a few μm. We introduce a steric-engineering ternary-solvent growth strategy to synthesize monolayer and few-layer A2MX4 hybrid perovskites with exceptionally large surface areas. By combining alcohol cosolvents with an amine additive, out-of-plane stacking is suppressed. Using (PEA)2CuCl4 as a model system, monolayers with lateral areas exceeding 1000 μm2 are achieved, representing a massive dimensional increase over conventional methods. Molecular dynamics and quantum-chemical calculations show that longer-chain alcohols reorganize precursor solvation, while solvent volatility prolongs edge-mediated precursor transport during annealing. This strategy demonstrates universal applicability across diverse organic spacer cations (PEA+, F-PEA+, PentA+), metal centers (Cu2+, Mn2+, Pb2+), and halides (Cl-, Br-, I-). The large lateral dimensions enable direct, solvent-free electrical contact fabrication via physical shadow masking, bypassing chemical degradation from solvents used in conventional lithography. Planar devices fabricated from isolated ultrathin (PEA)2PbI4 channels exhibit ultra-low dark currents down to the 10^-15 - 10^-13 A range, enabling femtowatt-to-picowatt static power consumption, ~ 0.2 pW at 5 V, a 250-fold reduction relative to drop-cast films, while maintaining a high light-to-dark current ratio of 4.3 x 102. This work establishes precise steric and solvation control as a paradigm for scalable, compositionally diverse, low-static-power monolayer 2D perovskite optoelectronics.

infographic.key_insight: Steric and solvation control enables hybrid perovskite monolayers exceeding 1000 μm² in lateral area, supporting lithography-free, low-static-power optoelectronics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Large ultrathin crystals permit solvent-free contacts through physical shadow masks, avoiding solvent-induced degradation associated with conventional lithography.
method: Use a ternary-solvent growth strategy combining alcohol cosolvents with an amine additive to suppress out-of-plane stacking.

infographic.paper_title: Universal Synthesis of Large-Area Hybrid Perovskite Monolayers Enabling Lithography-Free, Low-Static-Power Optoelectronics

title: Robust Anomalous Hall Effect in Epitaxial Cubic D0$_3$-Fe$_3$Ge Nanoplates Grown by Chemical Vapor Deposition
authors: Mingxuan Chen, Chao Chen, Siqi Jiang, Shuxiang Qiao, Hongyan Lu, Di Zhang
abstract: The iron-based ferromagnetic materials have emerged as a promising system for spintronics due to their high Curie temperatures and significant anomalous Hall effect (AHE) driven by Berry curvature. While there have been investigations into the epitaxial growth of non-layered iron-based ferromagnetic materials, the realization of high-quality single crystal thin films continues to be a formidable obstacle. Meanwhile, the issues such as grain boundary scattering further hinder their characterization and application. Here, we report the first chemical vapor deposition (CVD) synthesis of single-crystalline cubic D0$_3$-Fe$_3$Ge nanoplates. This compound represents a substantial departure from the conventional hexagonal phases typically observed in the Fe-Ge system. Structural characterizations confirm the cubic lattice and stoichiometric purity of the crystals. Structural analysis identifies a strong epitaxial effect, resulting in a giant compressive strain of ~4.16% at the interface that relaxes gradually toward the surface. The second-harmonic generation (SHG) signals might further reveal that such interfacial strain disrupted the inherent centro-symmetry of the cubic phase. SQUID magnetometry shows robust room-temperature ferromagnetism and clear magnetic anisotropy. Magneto-transport measurements reveal a robust AHE that remains stable at temperatures far exceeding room temperature. The scaling observed between the anomalous Hall resistance and longitudinal resistance strongly suggests that this effect is dominated by the intrinsic Berry curvature mechanism. Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the huge epitaxial strain induces band reconstructions and creates dense spin-orbit coupling gaps near the Fermi level, effectively doubling the anomalous Hall conductivity to match our experimental observations.

infographic.key_insight: CVD-grown single-crystalline cubic D0₃-Fe₃Ge nanoplates exhibit robust anomalous Hall behavior, with calculations linking epitaxial strain to enhanced Berry-curvature-driven conductivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These non-layered ferromagnetic nanoplates offer a potential route to spintronic devices operating above room temperature.
method: CVD growth and structural characterization of epitaxial cubic Fe₃Ge nanoplates.
SQUID magnetometry, Hall transport measurements, and second-harmonic generation probing.
DFT calculations of strain-induced band reconstruction and anomalous Hall conductivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Structural analysis indicates approximately 4.16% interfacial compressive strain, transport shows AHE persisting well above room temperature, and DFT predicts roughly doubled anomalous Hall conductivity consistent with experiment.
infographic.watch_item: Strain relaxes toward the surface, so controlling thickness and interface quality may be critical for reproducible device performance.
infographic.paper_title: Robust Anomalous Hall Effect in Epitaxial Cubic D0$_3$-Fe$_3$Ge Nanoplates Grown by Chemical Vapor Deposition

title: Electronic Screening as a Design Lever in La-Doped BaTiO$_3$: Coupled Polarization, Dielectric Response, and Optical Anisotropy
authors: Sikandar Azam, Muhammad Fareed, Qaiser Rafiq, Jan Minar, Abed Alataway
abstract: Donor substitution can tune the coupled ferroelectric, dielectric, electronic, and optical properties of perovskite oxides by modifying lattice distortions and electronic screening. We investigate these effects in La-doped BaTiO3 using density functional theory, density-functional perturbation theory, and the Berry-phase formalism for polarization. For a model with 12.5% La substitution at the Ba site, La incorporation induces anisotropic lattice contraction, reduces tetragonality and Ti off-centering, and weakens the energetic stabilization of the tetragonal ferroelectric phase. The accompanying reduction in polarization is associated with enhanced electronic screening and reduced anomalous Born effective charges. Phonon calculations indicate that the relaxed doped structure is dynamically stable, while hardening of a low-frequency polar mode is consistent with weakened ferroelectricity. The high-frequency dielectric response increases moderately, whereas the static dielectric response decreases as the lattice contribution is suppressed. Electronic-structure calculations show a Fermi-level shift toward the conduction band without mid-gap defect states. The optical spectra exhibit an absorption-edge shift consistent with a Burstein-Moss-type mechanism, enhanced near-edge transparency, and reduced birefringence. Together, these results suggest a microscopic connection between donor-induced screening, polar-mode hardening, reduced dynamical charges, polarization suppression, and decreased optical anisotropy. The conclusions apply to the investigated 12.5% composition; calculations at additional concentrations are needed to establish quantitative doping trends.

infographic.key_insight: At 12.5% La substitution in BaTiO₃, enhanced electronic screening is linked to weaker ferroelectric polarization, lower static dielectric response, and reduced optical anisotropy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: La donor substitution offers a route to tuning coupled dielectric and optical properties, with a trade-off between near-edge transparency and ferroelectric strength.
method: Density functional theory for structure, energetics, and electronic properties
Density-functional perturbation theory for phonons and dielectric response
Berry-phase calculations of polarization
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations show reduced tetragonality and anomalous Born effective charges, polar-mode hardening, dynamical stability, and an absorption-edge shift consistent with a Burstein–Moss-type mechanism.
infographic.watch_item: Results apply only to the modeled 12.5% La composition; additional concentrations are needed to establish quantitative doping trends.
infographic.paper_title: Electronic Screening as a Design Lever in La-Doped BaTiO$_3$: Coupled Polarization, Dielectric Response, and Optical Anisotropy

title: Crystal Structure Based Graph Neural Network And LLM Multi-Modal Approach for Material Magnetic Ordering Prediction
authors: Adam Zheng, April Zheng, Sheng Ran
abstract: AI/ML models are useful for the prediction of materials' properties. Recently, there has been great progress in developing Neural Network models to predict the properties of solids, molecules, and crystals, avoiding expensive and time-consuming laboratory testing. This study presents a novel AI/ML-based multi-modal approach to predict material magnetic ordering using material crystal structure information as input to a Graph Neural Network model (GNN) and semantic text descriptions of the material's properties and structure as input to a Large Language Model (LLM), before performing information fusion of the GNN and LLM outputs to predict material magnetic ordering in four classes (Non-magnetic, Ferromagnetic, Antiferromagnetic, Ferrimagnetic). The model is trained, validated, and tested on a dataset which is a combination of Materials Project dataset, Magndata dataset, and a set of uranium compounds with magnetic ordering determined in laboratory testing, with an 80/10/10 (training/validation/testing) data split. The proposed GNN and LLM multi-modal approach achieves better overall accuracy than both the standalone GNN and LLM approaches with three fusion strategies.

infographic.key_insight: Combining crystal-structure GNN outputs with material-description LLM outputs improves overall magnetic-ordering classification accuracy over either standalone model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support computational screening of magnetic materials before costly laboratory characterization.
method: Encode crystal structures with a graph neural network.
Process semantic descriptions of material properties and structure with a large language model.
Fuse outputs using three strategies to classify non-magnetic, ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, or ferrimagnetic ordering.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation uses combined Materials Project, Magndata, and laboratory-characterized uranium-compound data with an 80/10/10 training/validation/test split; the abstract reports improved overall accuracy but no numerical scores.
infographic.watch_item: Text descriptions should be checked for magnetic-label leakage to ensure that performance reflects predictive capability rather than disclosed answers.
infographic.paper_title: Crystal Structure Based Graph Neural Network And LLM Multi-Modal Approach for Material Magnetic Ordering Prediction

title: Challenging Atomistic Foundation Models on Disordered Carbons
authors: Joseph Hart, Samuel G. H. Brookes, Fabian L. Thiemann, Christoph Schran
abstract: Foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise broad transferability, yet their out-of-domain reliability is hard to establish. Here, we use pure and O/H-containing disordered carbon spanning multiple phases, competing hybridisations and porous frameworks to stress-test six popular foundation MLIPs. We first screen all six on density functional theory (DFT) energy and force errors and binding curves, then subject four to melt-quench-anneal molecular dynamics and evaluate the resulting structural observables. Binding curves and O/H-containing trajectories reveal unphysical extrapolation and dynamical failures that low DFT energy and force errors fail to reveal. Of the models tested, MACE-MH-1 is the most consistently robust, with low DFT errors and stable MD. Despite differing architectures, OMAT-based models share structural biases, highlighting the importance of training coverage. All four models generate structures of nanoporous carbon that reproduce the principal experimental and specialised carbon potential signatures. Incorporating O/H leaves short-range order largely unchanged but shifts pore-size distributions towards larger pores. These results emphasise the need for application-specific validation and extend molecular dynamics modelling of nanoporous carbon towards experimentally realistic structures.

infographic.key_insight: Low DFT energy and force errors do not guarantee reliable disordered-carbon simulations; MACE-MH-1 was the most consistently robust foundation MLIP tested.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Foundation MLIPs can support nanoporous-carbon modelling, but realistic O/H-containing systems require application-specific stability and structural validation.
method: Screen six foundation MLIPs using DFT energy and force errors and binding curves.
Run melt-quench-anneal molecular dynamics with four models.
Evaluate structural observables across pure and O/H-containing disordered carbons.
infographic.evidence_signal: All four MD-tested models reproduced principal experimental and specialised-potential signatures of nanoporous carbon, while binding curves and O/H-containing trajectories exposed failures missed by low DFT errors.
infographic.watch_item: Shared structural biases among OMAT-based models suggest that training coverage can limit reliability despite architectural differences.
infographic.paper_title: Challenging Atomistic Foundation Models on Disordered Carbons

title: Anomalous polar chains in halide perovskites
authors: Erik Fransson, Apinya Ngoipala, Priyanka Deswal, Ethan Berger, Nicholas C. Bristowe, Paul Erhart
abstract: Local polar distortions, their collective ordering, and their field-driven reversal have been studied extensively in ferroelectric perovskites for decades. Here we identify an unusual behavior in the ferroelectric halide perovskite CsGeBr3 using large-scale molecular dynamics with first-principles-trained interatomic potentials. In its nominally cubic phase the Ge off-centering forms one-dimensional polar chains that extend over at least tens of nanometers and relax on nanosecond timescales, four orders of magnitude slower than in BaTiO3 and PbTiO3, with CsSnBr3 in between. The cubic CsGeBr3 phase is a dynamically disordered state in which oppositely polarized chains flip throughout the crystal, and a long-lived one-dimensional local polarization coexists with zero net polarization. A simple three-dimensional perovskite thus hosts long-ranged one-dimensional polar correlations with remarkably slow dynamics. In the ferroelectric phase the same chains set a one-dimensional switching mechanism, in which the polarization reverses chain by chain.

infographic.key_insight: CsGeBr3 hosts long-lived, one-dimensional polar chains even in its nominally cubic phase, where opposing local polarizations yield zero net polarization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Chain-by-chain polarization reversal could inform switching models for halide-perovskite ferroelectric devices, although device performance is not established here.
method: Large-scale molecular dynamics with first-principles-trained interatomic potentials
Analysis of local polar correlations and relaxation dynamics
Investigation of field-driven polarization reversal
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show polar chains extending at least tens of nanometers and relaxing on nanosecond timescales—four orders of magnitude slower than in BaTiO3 and PbTiO3, with CsSnBr3 intermediate.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports simulation evidence; experimental validation of chain lengths, lifetimes, and switching behavior remains important.
infographic.paper_title: Anomalous polar chains in halide perovskites

title: How good are universal MLIPs for alloys? A benchmark is only as trustworthy as its controls
authors: Gus L. W. Hart, Jacob N. Pursley
abstract: Universal machine-learned interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) are ranked by their formation-energy error against a DFT database, as if that database were ground truth, but independent DFT databases disagree. We benchmark fourteen uMLIPs on 1.45 million ordered intermetallics against AFLOW, which none trained on, and compare every energy and stability error with that disagreement. For half the structures, AFLOW, Alexandria, and OQMD differ by less than 6-8 meV/atom, but a minority differ by far more, raising the average to 16-30. That disagreement sets a floor on any model's measurable error. Re-referenced, the best uMLIP agrees with AFLOW as closely as Alexandria does, and the next four sit 2-7 meV/atom above the floor. Once broken elemental references are screened, the energy and stability rankings agree almost everywhere. Three apparent model failures shrink or vanish under the right control: poorly correlated shear moduli, thousands of "bad" DFT references, and the leader's inflated lead.

infographic.key_insight: Universal alloy potentials can approach cross-database DFT agreement, making benchmark controls essential for interpreting model rankings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For alloy screening, checking elemental references and DFT database disagreement helps distinguish model errors from benchmark artifacts.
method: Benchmark 14 universal ML interatomic potentials on 1.45 million ordered intermetallics against AFLOW, unseen during training.
Compare energy and stability errors with disagreement among AFLOW, Alexandria, and OQMD.
Re-reference energies and screen broken elemental references to test ranking robustness.
infographic.evidence_signal: Half the structures show DFT disagreement below 6–8 meV/atom, but averages reach 16–30 meV/atom; after re-referencing, the best model matches Alexandria’s agreement with AFLOW.
infographic.watch_item: DFT database disagreement limits measurable accuracy, so small ranking differences should not be treated as definitive model superiority.
infographic.paper_title: How good are universal MLIPs for alloys? A benchmark is only as trustworthy as its controls

title: Strain-induced structural transformations in hexagonal monolayer boron nitride. A density functional study
authors: O. Bystrenko, B. Ilkiv, S. Petrovska, O. Foia, T. Bystrenko, O. Khyzhun
abstract: In this work we theoretically study the structural transformations occurring in monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) subjected to strong deformations. The first-principle computer simulations are based on the density functional theory employing the pseudopotentials with the exchange-correlation energy given in Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof form. Depending on the direction and the type of the strain, the simulations reveal different types of structural transformations in two-dimensional (2D) h-BN associated with the elastic failure. It is found that, under certain shear strains, there can form an ordered 2D orthorhombic phase with the 2D layer space symmetry pmmm. Thermal stability of the latter up to ~900 K is demonstrated by first-principle Born-Oppenheimer molecular dynamics. The examination of electronic structure indicates that, in contrast to the conventional h-BN, which is an insulator with the wide band gap, the predicted orthorhombic phase is expected to be a semiconductor with the narrow band gap of ~ 0.65 eV.

infographic.key_insight: DFT predicts that certain shear strains transform monolayer hexagonal boron nitride into an ordered orthorhombic pmmm phase with a narrow band gap of approximately 0.65 eV.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Strain-induced phase transformation could enable band-gap engineering of monolayer boron nitride from a wide-gap insulator toward a narrow-gap semiconductor.
method: First-principles DFT using pseudopotentials and PBE exchange–correlation.
Structural and electronic analysis under different strain types and directions.
First-principles Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics for thermal stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations predict an orthorhombic phase under certain shear strains, demonstrate thermal stability up to approximately 900 K, and estimate its band gap at approximately 0.65 eV.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental realization remains unverified, and the transformation occurs under strong deformation associated with elastic failure.
infographic.paper_title: Strain-induced structural transformations in hexagonal monolayer boron nitride. A density functional study

title: The Critical 2D KPZ Process
authors: Quentin Berger, Francesco Caravenna, Jeremy Clark, Alexander Dunlap, Yu Gu, Ziyang Liu
abstract: This work constructs a non-trivial solution to the ill-defined two-dimensional Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation at criticality: a distribution-valued stochastic process on the plane, which we call the Critical 2D KPZ Process. It arises as the limit in law of centred log partition functions of two-dimensional Gaussian directed polymers at criticality, viewed as discretised KPZ solutions. It is also a measurable function of the Critical 2D Stochastic Heat Flow (SHF) via a renormalised Cole-Hopf transformation, obtained as the limit of the centred logarithm of the spatially mollified SHF as the smoothing is removed. The Critical 2D KPZ process is non-Gaussian and its covariance displays a log-log blow-up near the diagonal. Gaussian fluctuations emerge when averaging on shrinking spatial scales. The results presented here were obtained through extensive interactions with generative AI (ChatGPT 5.5, 5.6 and 6); see Appendix C for more details. The proof builds on key recent and older advances in our field, combined in novel ways with substantial AI input. We view this manuscript as a "community project" that represents more than a decade's collective effort. We have worked on making the presentation as accessible as possible, highlighting the main ideas and their relations to the literature.

infographic.key_insight: The paper constructs a non-Gaussian, distribution-valued Critical 2D KPZ Process, giving a rigorous meaning to the otherwise ill-defined two-dimensional KPZ equation at criticality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result advances mathematical foundations for stochastic interface-growth models potentially relevant to materials science, rather than demonstrating a materials-discovery application.
method: Take the limit in law of centered log partition functions of critical two-dimensional Gaussian directed polymers.
Construct a renormalized Cole–Hopf transformation from the Critical 2D Stochastic Heat Flow.
Analyze covariance singularities and fluctuations under shrinking-scale spatial averaging.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical results: non-Gaussianity, a log-log covariance blow-up near the diagonal, and Gaussian fluctuations under shrinking-scale spatial averaging; no experimental datasets or numerical benchmarks are described.
infographic.watch_item: This is a distribution-valued theoretical construction, not a directly implementable materials model; numerical approximation and application-specific validation are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: The Critical 2D KPZ Process

title: GANet: A Lightweight Group Attention Network for Plant Disease Identification on Embedded Systems
authors: Anubhab Tripathi, Bibek Das, Asfak Ali, Sheli Shinha Chaudhuri
abstract: Global warming and climate change are major catalysts for plant diseases, significantly affecting food production worldwide. Addressing this issue requires continuous monitoring and early detection of plant diseases. While recent advancements in deep learning offer potential solutions, most models demand high processing power and struggle to perform efficiently on low-end electronic hardware. Furthermore, many existing works focus on specific crop diseases, limiting their broader applicability. This paper presents a lightweight Group Equivariance Attention Network (GANet) designed for the prediction and monitoring of 38 types of plant diseases. GANet introduces a novel Group Attention block and Group-Wise Feature Fusion block, making it both sparse and efficient. With only 0.001M parameters, the model achieves an impressive 99.99% accuracy on the PlantVillage dataset. Additionally, GANet is optimized for deployment on edge devices such as the Raspberry Pi 4b and Jetson Nano, where it reaches 5 FPS and 11 FPS, respectively, demonstrating its potential for real-time plant disease monitoring on low-power devices.

infographic.key_insight: GANet reports 99.99% accuracy on PlantVillage with only 0.001M parameters, targeting lightweight plant disease identification.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its compact architecture supports on-device crop monitoring where computing power and energy are constrained.
method: Lightweight Group Equivariance Attention Network.
Group Attention block for feature processing.
Group-Wise Feature Fusion block for sparse, efficient computation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation across 38 plant disease types on PlantVillage and deployment speeds of 5 FPS on Raspberry Pi 4b and 11 FPS on Jetson Nano.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on diverse field images remains unestablished by the abstract; near-perfect benchmark accuracy may not translate to real-world conditions.
infographic.paper_title: GANet: A Lightweight Group Attention Network for Plant Disease Identification on Embedded Systems

title: Strain-Induced Interfacial Bond Evolution and Facet-dependent Strain Response of Electronic Properties in Oxidized Silicon Nanowires
authors: Yasir Mahmood, Daniel Wines, Viviana Dovale-Farelo, Kamal Choudhary, Lucas M Hale
abstract: Silicon nanowires (Si NWs) have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation nanoelectronic devices due to their tunable electronic properties, and compatibility with aggressive scaling requirements. The integration of strain further enhances their performance by modulating carrier mobility, band structure, and transport behavior without altering material chemistry. Within the NW, the silicon-silicon dioxide (Si-SiO$_{2}$) interface serves as a critical region where strain redistribution and suboxide bonding collectively influence the mechanical and electronic response. Here, we combine reactive force field molecular dynamics and first-principles calculations to investigate how oxidation-induced interfacial structure and crystallographic facet orientation govern strain-dependent bond evolution and facet-dependent strain response of electronic properties in oxidized Si NWs. Simulated dry thermal oxidation generates chemically realistic Si-SiO$_{2}$ interfaces, enabling direct characterization of bond order redistribution and stress gradient development across the interface under tensile strain. Interfacial Si-Si bonds exhibit elongation and reduced bond order associated with partial oxidation states, leading to localized stress concentration and preferential bond rupture. Complementary density functional theory calculations on facet-specific models reveal that orientation-dependent interfacial bonding modulates facet-dependent strain response of electronic properties. Together, these results establish a direct coupling between interfacial suboxide chemistry, mechanical deformation, and electronic structure, providing atomistic insight into strain-modulated behavior at oxidized silicon interfaces in faceted NWs.

infographic.key_insight: Interfacial suboxide chemistry couples tensile deformation to bond weakening in oxidized silicon nanowires, while crystallographic facet orientation shapes the electronic response to strain.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling interface chemistry and facet orientation could help tune strain-dependent electronic behavior while managing localized mechanical failure in silicon nanowire devices.
method: Simulate dry thermal oxidation with reactive force field molecular dynamics.
Track interfacial bond evolution and stress gradients under tensile strain.
Use density functional theory on facet-specific models to probe electronic response.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show elongated, lower-bond-order interfacial Si–Si bonds associated with partial oxidation, localized stress and preferential rupture, alongside facet-dependent electronic responses in first-principles calculations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports computational findings without experimental validation or quantitative device-performance benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: Strain-Induced Interfacial Bond Evolution and Facet-dependent Strain Response of Electronic Properties in Oxidized Silicon Nanowires
